title: Centered 3-Employee Moving Average
description:
Order employees by hire date. For each one, report the average salary across **the employee hired just before them, themselves, and the employee hired just after them** (a centered 3-row window — fewer than 3 rows at either edge is fine).

Name the columns `name` and `centered_avg` (rounded to 2 decimals). Return the result in any order.
hint: "Just before and just after" is an explicit frame, not the default — `ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING`. The default frame (nothing after ORDER BY) would only look backward, never forward.
outputExplanation: Eve (first hire) averages only with Ava, and Hal (last hire) averages only with Gia. Everyone else averages with their immediate predecessor and successor.

title: Each Row Shows Its Department's Top Earner
description:
For every employee, report their own name alongside the name of the **highest-paid person in their own department** — repeated on every row of that department.

Name the columns `name` and `dept_top_earner`. Return the result in any order.
hint: FIRST_VALUE always returns the first row of the frame — order the partition by salary descending so "first" means "highest paid", and use a full-partition frame so every row (not just later ones) sees the same answer.
outputExplanation: Ava ($150k) is Engineering's top earner — her name appears on all four Engineering rows. Eve ($130k) appears on all three Sales rows. Hal is HR's only employee.

title: Split Employees Into Salary Thirds
description:
Order all employees by salary and split them into 3 roughly equal-sized groups (lowest-paid third, middle third, highest-paid third).

Name the columns `name` and `salary_third` (1, 2 or 3). Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY salary, id) AS salary_third
FROM employees;
hint: NTILE(n) just numbers the rows into n as-equal-as-possible buckets in ORDER BY order — it has nothing to do with the salary values themselves, only their rank.
outputExplanation: The 8 employees are split into three groups: Hal/Finn/Gia (group 1), Dan/Ben/Cara (group 2), and Eve/Ava (group 3).

title: Cumulative Hires, Counting Same-Day Hires Together
description:
Report a running count of employees hired up to and including each hire date — but if several employees were hired on the **same date**, they must all show the same cumulative count (the count as of that whole date, not partway through it).

Name the columns `name`, `hire_date` and `hires_so_far`. Return the result in any order.
hint: This is the real difference between RANGE and ROWS: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts physical rows up to this one, so two people hired the same day would get *different* counts depending on row order. RANGE treats every row with an equal ORDER BY value as one "peer group" and gives them all the same result.
outputExplanation: Eve and Ava get counts 1 and 2. Ben and Cara (same hire date) both get count 4. The remaining hires continue from 5 through 8.

title: Salary Percentile Rank Within Department
description:
For every employee, report their salary's percentile rank **within their own department** using `PERCENT_RANK()`, rounded to 4 decimals. It ranges from 0 (the lowest paid in the department) to 1 (the highest paid).

Name the columns `name` and `pct_rank`. Return the result in any order.
hint: PERCENT_RANK() is (rank - 1) / (rows in partition - 1) — a department with only one employee always gives that employee 0, since there's no spread to rank against.
outputExplanation: Dan is at the 0th percentile in Engineering, Ben and Cara at 0.3333, and Ava at the 100th. In Sales, Finn is at 0, Gia at 0.5 and Eve at 1. Hal (only employee in HR) is at 0 by convention.

title: Trailing 3-Hire Average, Explicit Bounds
description:
Order employees by hire date. For each one, report the average salary across **themselves and the two people hired immediately before them** (fewer than 3 for the first couple of hires is fine — average over whatever's available).

Name the columns `name` and `trailing_avg` (rounded to 2 decimals). Return the result in any order.
hint: Contrast with the centered-average problem: this one only looks backward (`2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`), never forward — a genuinely trailing window, the kind you'd use for a running average you could compute in real time as hires happen.
outputExplanation: Eve (first hire) shows just her own salary. Ava averages with Eve. From Ben onward each row averages with the two preceding hires. Hal averages with Dan and Gia for $80,000.

title: Salary Two Hires Before, With A Default
description:
Within each department, order employees by hire date. For each one, report the salary of the person hired **two hires before them** in that same department. If there isn't one (too early in the department's history), report `0` instead of `NULL`.

Name the columns `name` and `salary_two_hires_ago`. Return the result in any order.
hint: LAG takes three arguments: the column, how many rows back, and a default to use instead of NULL when that row doesn't exist — most people only ever use the first argument.
outputExplanation: In Engineering, Ava and Ben have no hire two positions before them and get 0. Cara gets Ava's $150k and Dan gets Ben's $120k. In Sales, Eve and Finn get 0, Gia gets Eve's $130k. Hal alone in HR gets 0.

title: Salary Quartiles When Many Salaries Tie
description:
Split all employees into 4 salary quartiles using `NTILE(4)`. Several employees may share the exact same salary — order by salary, then by `id` to keep the split deterministic.

Name the columns `name` and `quartile`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary, id) AS quartile
FROM employees;
hint: NTILE does not know or care that several rows are tied on salary — it splits strictly by row position in ORDER BY order. Two employees earning the identical salary can easily land in different quartiles. Without a tie-breaker like `id`, which one gets which quartile isn't even well-defined.
outputExplanation: The 8 employees are split into 4 quartiles of 2 each: Hal/Finn (Q1), Gia/Dan (Q2), Ben/Cara (Q3), Eve/Ava (Q4). Tied employees can land in different quartiles in other datasets.

title: Sum Of Prices Within $10
description:
For every product, report the sum of the prices of all products priced **within $10 of it in either direction** (including itself), using a numeric `RANGE` frame — not a self-join.

Name the columns `name`, `price` and `nearby_sum` (rounded to 2 decimals). Return the result in any order.
hint: RANGE frame bounds can be numeric offsets on the ORDER BY value itself, not just row counts — "10 PRECEDING" here means "price is at least 10 less", not "10 rows back". SQLite requires the ORDER BY to be a single numeric column for this to work.
outputExplanation: No two products are within $10 of each other, so each nearby_sum equals the product's own price. A hidden test with two $50 products shows them combining into a sum of $100.

title: First And Last Order Date Per Customer — The LAST_VALUE Trap
description:
For every order, report that customer's very first order date and very last order date, alongside the current order's own date.

Name the columns `customer`, `order_date`, `first_order_date` and `last_order_date`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT c.name AS customer, o.order_date,
  FIRST_VALUE(o.order_date) OVER (
    PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_date, o.id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS first_order_date,
  LAST_VALUE(o.order_date) OVER (
    PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_date, o.id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS last_order_date
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
hint: This is the single most common LAST_VALUE mistake: with just an ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the *default* frame is "UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW" — which makes LAST_VALUE return the current row's own value every time, not the true last row. You must widen the frame to the whole partition explicitly.
outputExplanation: Ada's rows all show first_order_date as 2022-01-10 and last_order_date as 2023-01-02. The same consistency holds for Bo and Cy.
